# Field guide

The design basics, explained with pins from my own library. Every principle has a way to check it, the usual mistakes, and a small study to practise it. The design-review skill uses the same names, so its notes point back here.

## The idea

<a id="one-idea"></a>
### One organising idea

**The site is about one thing, and everything follows from it.**

Good sites aren't a collection of nice effects. They have one idea that decides the layout, the type, the motion and what gets left out. Obys is one centre line with a lens on it; Gionatan Nese is a slow cloud of objects. Once you have the idea, most design questions answer themselves: does this help the idea or not?

**How to check:** Say the site in one sentence. Then go through every section and effect and ask whether it comes from that sentence. Anything that doesn't is decoration, and can usually go.

**Usual mistakes**

- Starting from a list of effects you like instead of from the subject of the site
- An idea that would fit any client equally well (then it's a style, not an idea)
- Adding a second big idea halfway through because the first one feels too simple

**Practise:** Take one pin you love and write its organising idea in one sentence. Then sketch the same idea for a completely different subject (a bakery, a record label, a dentist). (`pnpm kit study one-idea`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-obys` Obys — a white page, one strip of work and a lens that frames it: One horizontal line organises the whole page: the list, the frame, the number all hang off it
- `lib-gn` Gionatan Nese — a portfolio as a slowly turning cloud of objects: No headline, no scroll: the work as small floating objects is the whole idea
- `lib-koko-portal` Kokopako — the card is a window into a dark world: Light and dark are one 3D world; the page transition pulls you through the window
- `iva-n-claude-design` Claude Design output: What happens without an idea: generic, and the work got lost

<a id="content-first"></a>
### Design with the real content

**The real words and images shape the design, not lorem ipsum.**

Layouts are made for content. A hero that works with a three-word name breaks with a long one; a grid made for 12 projects looks empty with 4. Designers collect the real copy, images and numbers first and design around them. The content also gives you ideas: Iva's dither effect only worked once it printed her own projects.

**How to check:** Is there any placeholder text or stock image left? Count the real things (projects, products, words in the bio) and check the layout still works with the longest and the shortest one.

**Usual mistakes**

- Designing with lorem ipsum and finding out late that the copy doesn't fit
- A layout built for 20 projects when there are 5
- Writing the copy last, so it fills space instead of saying something

**Practise:** Rewrite one site's hero in three versions: 4 words, 12 words and 30 words. Lay out all three in the same grid and see which layout survives all of them. (`pnpm kit study content-first`)

**In my pins**

- `iva-d-name` Name only in the nav; hero introduces her: A copy decision changed the hero: the name moved to the nav, the hero introduces her instead
- `lib-idea-mix` Graphic hover effects, tied to the content: Borrow the technique, then feed it the site's own content
- `lib-and2es` AND2ES — a studio site that is almost only the work, on white: The work carries the page; the one line of copy only appears in the preloader
- `lib-ss` Short Sentence — plain UI, colourful product: All the colour comes from the product photos, not from the interface

<a id="signature"></a>
### One signature moment

**One thing people remember, and calm everywhere else.**

Memorable sites usually have one moment people describe to a friend: the liquid wordmark, the cigarette that burns as you scroll, the dotted reveal. Everything around it stays quiet so it can stand out. Three signature moments on one page cancel each other out.

**How to check:** What would a visitor describe to a friend afterwards? If you can't name one thing, there's no signature. If you can name four, pick one and calm down the others.

**Usual mistakes**

- Every section has its own big effect, so nothing stands out
- The signature moment is hidden below the fold or behind a click
- The moment is impressive but has nothing to do with the site's subject

**Practise:** Pick a plain one-page site you know and design only its signature moment: one interaction that comes from what the site is about. Build it as a single HTML file. (`pnpm kit study signature`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-sapo` Mount Sapo — liquid wordmark under the cursor: The giant wordmark smears under the mouse; the rest of the shop is flat colour blocks
- `lib-gass-cig` GASS Records — a cigarette that burns down as you scroll: A scroll progress bar turned into a cigarette: on-brand and funny
- `iva-d-reveal` Dotted work reveal ("looks awesome"): Iva's own: her projects printed as dots, the pointer uncovers the real image
- `lib-an` A Noche Sone — "Build your outfit" dress-up doll: A dress-up doll as the shop's signature; one GSAP Draggable call

<a id="borrow-technique"></a>
### Borrow the technique, not the look

**Take how something works, then make it look like this site.**

This is the kit's manifesto. Copying a site's whole look makes yours a lesser version of it. Taking one technique (a dither, a mask, a grid that becomes a transition) and feeding it the new site's content and colours makes it yours. Never take more than one thing from one source site.

**How to check:** The copy test: put your page next to the source. Would people think it's the same site? Then rework it more: new content, new form, new colours, different timing.

**Usual mistakes**

- Taking a site's layout, type, palette and signature motion together
- Keeping the source's colours because they 'just work'
- Using an effect because it's cool, without asking what it shows on this site

**Practise:** Pick one pin's technique and rebuild it with completely different content and colours. Write down what you changed and why. (`pnpm kit study borrow-technique`)

**In my pins**

- `iva-n-dither` Plain dither + trail copied from Aspen: The rejected version: Aspen's dither copied as it was
- `iva-d-reveal` Dotted work reveal ("looks awesome"): The kept version: the same technique printing Iva's work
- `lib-aspen` Aspen Search — dithered hero with a fluid trail: The source the technique came from

## Layout

<a id="hierarchy"></a>
### Hierarchy

**The eye knows what to read first, second and third.**

Every screen should have a clear order. You make it with size, weight, colour, position and space. You don't need all of them: AND2ES sets everything at 11px and makes the order with black or grey fills only; Obys makes the current project black and everything else light grey.

**How to check:** The squint test: blur your eyes (or the screenshot). Can you still tell what's first, second and third? If everything has the same weight, nothing leads.

**Usual mistakes**

- Everything bold, big or coloured, so nothing stands out
- Two things fighting to be first (a big name and a big headline)
- Using five ways of emphasis at once (size + colour + caps + underline + box)

**Practise:** Set a page with one font size only and make the hierarchy with weight, fill or position. Then do the same page with size only. (`pnpm kit study hierarchy`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-and2es-pills` AND2ES — everything set in 11px black pills: One tiny size for everything; hierarchy comes only from the black or grey fill
- `lib-obys-list` Obys — a project list that turns so the current one sits on the centre line: Current title black, the rest #c9c9c9: you read one line
- `lib-gn-nav` Gionatan Nese — pill nav where only the current page has a name: Only the current page has a name; the others shrink to numbers
- `iva-d-name` Name only in the nav; hero introduces her: Two big names fought for first place; one moved to the nav

<a id="scale-contrast"></a>
### Contrast of scale

**Very big next to very small, rarely medium.**

Creative sites often feel designed because of extreme size jumps: a wordmark the full width of the screen above 11px body text. Medium sizes everywhere look like a template. A strong contrast also does the hierarchy for you.

**How to check:** Compare your biggest and smallest type. A ratio under about 4× usually feels flat on a creative site. Count your sizes: more than 5 or 6 means the scale isn't doing its job.

**Usual mistakes**

- Headings only a little bigger than the body text
- Lots of in-between sizes (17, 18, 20, 22, 24…)
- Huge type that also shouts in colour and weight, so there's no quiet part

**Practise:** Make a poster-style page with only two sizes: one huge, one tiny. No medium allowed. (`pnpm kit study scale-contrast`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-obys-about` Obys — about page ends on a full-width wordmark: Whisper-small body, then the wordmark the full width of the screen as the full stop
- `lib-mis` Made in Slovenia — marquees as section dividers: One grotesk at extreme size contrast
- `lib-muller` helloMuller — "catalogue of work" ledger: Huge condensed headline over small mono meta
- `lib-bleib-goo` Bleibtgleich — "melt" line reveal on headings: Huge Akzidenz on a strict grid

<a id="space"></a>
### Space

**Empty space groups things and gives them importance.**

Space isn't left over, it's a material. Things that are close read as a group; things far apart read as separate (that's called proximity). A small object alone in a lot of white looks precious. Most beginner layouts are too tight inside and too loose between the wrong things.

**How to check:** Are related things closer to each other than to unrelated things? Is there one spacing scale (for example 4, 8, 16, 24, 48, 96) or lots of random values?

**Usual mistakes**

- Same spacing everywhere, so nothing groups
- Filling every empty area because it 'looks unfinished'
- Random margins (13px here, 22px there) instead of a scale

**Practise:** Take a busy page and remove a third of it. Use the freed space to group what's left, without adding lines or boxes. (`pnpm kit study space`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-gn` Gionatan Nese — a portfolio as a slowly turning cloud of objects: Small objects in a lot of white: restraint makes the work feel precious
- `lib-and2es-index` AND2ES — index table with an image strip that slides up on hover: No rules between rows; 21px rows and alignment do the grouping
- `lib-grau` Elias Grau — info column + one looping reel panel: An info column and one panel: two groups, nothing else

<a id="grid"></a>
### Grid

**An invisible structure that makes the page feel intentional.**

A grid is a set of columns (and a gutter and a margin) that everything lines up to. It's why some pages feel calm even when they're full. Once you have one, breaking it on purpose becomes a tool. Some sites even show the grid as part of the look.

**How to check:** Turn on the grid overlay (G on the kit's Grids page, or the wireframe tool). Do edges line up with columns? Are breaks from the grid deliberate?

**Usual mistakes**

- No grid, so every section has its own widths
- A grid on desktop that falls apart on the phone
- Breaking the grid everywhere, so it's no longer a break

**Practise:** Lay out the same three projects on three different grids: 4 columns no gutter, 8 columns with one axis line, 12 columns asymmetric. Which one fits which mood? (`pnpm kit study grid`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-aspen-grid` Aspen Search — edge-to-edge grid, 1px rules: No gutters, 1px rules, content bottom-left: the grid is the look
- `lib-bleib-goo` Bleibtgleich — "melt" line reveal on headings: A strict 8-column grid with one vertical rule
- `lib-kaspar` Maximilian Kaspar — page transition from the grid columns: A visible 4-column hairline grid that also becomes the page transition
- `lib-donut` Donut Studio — everything below the hero: An asymmetric 12-column collage that still lines up

<a id="rhythm"></a>
### Rhythm and repetition

**The same pattern repeated makes dense pages feel tidy.**

When every project row or card follows the same pattern, a page can hold a lot without feeling messy. Repetition is also what makes a break in the pattern noticeable. GASS repeats marquee rows but gives each one a different speed, so the rhythm is alive.

**How to check:** Look at a list or grid section: does every item follow the same pattern (same spacing, same caption position, same image height)? Are the exceptions on purpose?

**Usual mistakes**

- Every card a little different, so the page looks unplanned
- Repetition with no variation anywhere, so long pages get boring
- Section spacing that changes from section to section

**Practise:** Design one project row (image + caption + meta) and repeat it 10 times. Then add one deliberate variation every fourth row. (`pnpm kit study rhythm`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-and2es-work` AND2ES — work page: numbered rows of meta pills over image strips: A dense contact sheet that stays tidy because every row has the same rhythm
- `lib-muller` helloMuller — "catalogue of work" ledger: Every project gets the same white info card, then a mosaic
- `lib-gass-rows` GASS Records — stacked marquee rows, out of sync: Same marquee rows, each at its own random speed

## Type and colour

<a id="type-voices"></a>
### Type voices

**One family, or a deliberate pair, each with a job.**

Type does most of the work on a creative site. Use one family, or two (or three) faces that each have a clear job: a neutral workhorse for reading, a voice for character. Pair faces that are clearly different, not almost the same. Big type usually wants tight leading and slightly negative tracking; body text wants more air.

**How to check:** How many families are on the page? Can you name each one's job? Are big headings set tighter (leading under 1, tracking slightly negative) and body text looser (leading 1.4–1.6)?

**Usual mistakes**

- Two faces that are almost the same (two similar grotesks)
- A decorative face used for long text
- Default leading and tracking on huge headings, so they look loose

**Practise:** Set the same paragraph and heading in three pairings: one family only, a grotesk + a serif at the same small size, and a neutral face + one ornate display face. (`pnpm kit study type-voices`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-gn-type` Gionatan Nese — a grotesk and a serif at the same small size: A grotesk and a serif at the same small size, paired on one line
- `lib-gass-type` GASS Records — three type voices: grotesk, swash, chunky: Three voices: a neutral grotesk, a swash script, a chunky badge face
- `iva-d-type` One typeface: Inter Tight everywhere: Iva's decision: one typeface everywhere
- `lib-koko-split` Kokopako — every letter cut between a serif and a sans: Two faces stitched inside each letter: pairing as the signature

<a id="colour-roles"></a>
### Colour roles

**Few colours, each with a job, and text that reads.**

Give each colour a role: paper (background), ink (text), accent (the one that draws the eye), mist (a quiet fill), muted (secondary text). That's how the kit's themes work. Loud palettes still work when the roles are strict: GASS uses five flat colours and rules for which text goes on which band. Text needs enough contrast to read: 4.5:1 for body text.

**How to check:** List every colour on the page. Can you name each one's role? Check contrast for every text colour on every background it sits on (the specimen page and the design review do this).

**Usual mistakes**

- The accent used everywhere, so it no longer draws the eye
- Brand colours that are too dark or too light for text on them
- A different colour for every section, with no rule

**Practise:** Take one palette from a pin and write its rules: which colour is the background, which carries text, which is only for fills. Then apply those rules to a new palette. (`pnpm kit study colour-roles`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-gass-color` GASS Records — red, forest green, lilac, powder blue, peach: Five flat colours used as whole bands, with strict text rules
- `lib-muller` helloMuller — "catalogue of work" ledger: One bold colour carries the whole brand
- `iva-d-palette` White, black and her green only: Tried colour blocks, went back to white, black and one green
- `iva-n-red` Brightened Gabagool red: A brand red too dark for black text

<a id="restraint"></a>
### Restraint

**Every element has to earn its place.**

The sites in this library that feel most expensive use very little: one or two colours, one or two faces, one effect. Restraint isn't the same as boring. It leaves room for the one thing that matters to be loud.

**How to check:** Remove something (a colour, an effect, a section, a line). Is the page worse? If not, leave it out.

**Usual mistakes**

- Adding something every time a page feels plain
- Keeping every idea because each one is nice on its own
- Decoration (lines, boxes, icons) doing the job that space should do

**Practise:** Rebuild a section with half the elements: one colour, one face, no lines. Then add back only what you miss. (`pnpm kit study restraint`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-and2es` AND2ES — a studio site that is almost only the work, on white: Almost only the work, #fff, #000 and #e6e6e6, everything 11px
- `iva-d-palette` White, black and her green only: Back to white, black and one green
- `iva-n-progress` Progress bar in the full-screen hero: A small extra UI element that wasn't needed: 'Please no.'

## Motion and interaction

<a id="motion-meaning"></a>
### Motion with a job

**Every animation tells the visitor something.**

Good motion explains: where something came from, what changed, what to look at, that the page is loading something worth waiting for. Motion without a job is just movement, and it gets tiring fast. Easing and timing matter as much as the effect: most of this kit uses an out-expo ease and durations around 0.6–1.2s.

**How to check:** For each animation, finish the sentence 'this motion tells you that…'. Turn on reduced motion: does the page still work and make sense?

**Usual mistakes**

- Everything fades up on scroll, so motion says nothing
- Animations that delay reading (long intros on every visit)
- Linear or default easing, which looks mechanical
- Motion that makes the content harder to see (too fast, too round, too scattered)

**Practise:** Animate the same card three ways: one that explains where it came from, one that shows it's selected, one that's only decoration. Compare how they feel. (`pnpm kit study motion-meaning`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-k95-hover` k95 — hover slows the whole scene: Hover slows the whole scene down so the busy 3D becomes readable
- `lib-obys-horizontal` Obys — the strip turns on its side, and titles reveal their image: The layout change itself is the animation
- `lib-and2es-intro` AND2ES — preloader line, image flipbook, then the stack fans out into the ring: The loading wait becomes a preview of every project
- `iva-n-funnel` Round disc / scattered funnel swirl: Motion that hid the work: too round, then too scattered
- `iva-n-stack` Stacking cards work layout: Stacking cards: movement with no reason for this site

<a id="wayfinding"></a>
### Wayfinding

**Visitors always know where they are and how to get back.**

Creative navigation is fine as long as people don't get lost. The best pins turn navigation into a progress indicator: the list shows where you are, the nav names only the current page. Moving between pages should feel like zooming in, not like leaving.

**How to check:** From any page, can you tell where you are and get back in one step? Do project pages have their own URL you can share? Does Escape close overlays, and does the back button work?

**Usual mistakes**

- Hiding the nav behind a clever interaction
- Overlays that can't be shared or closed with Escape
- Case pages with a completely different layout from the home page

**Practise:** Design a navigation that's also a progress indicator for a list of 10 projects. (`pnpm kit study wayfinding`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-gn-nav` Gionatan Nese — pill nav where only the current page has a name: Only the current page has a name
- `lib-obys-list` Obys — a project list that turns so the current one sits on the centre line: The list is the navigation and the progress indicator
- `lib-sapo-sticky` Mount Sapo — stacked sections + fisheye index: The section list scales the current name up
- `lib-obys-project` Obys — case page: the lens closes, the work becomes a column on the right: The case page keeps the home's centre line: arriving feels like zooming in
- `iva-d-drawer` Project drawer with its own link: A drawer with its own URL, Escape closes, previous / next

## Craft

<a id="for-everyone"></a>
### Works for everyone

**Readable, usable on a phone, with a keyboard and without motion.**

A creative site still has to be readable and usable. That means text contrast, tap targets big enough for fingers, a version for people who turn motion off, focus outlines for keyboard users, and real text behind any WebGL. Designing the phone version early is part of the design, not a later fix.

**How to check:** Look at it on a phone. Tab through it with the keyboard. Turn on reduced motion. Check contrast. The design review runs all of these.

**Usual mistakes**

- Hover-only interactions with no touch version
- Text drawn only in a canvas, so it can't be read by screen readers or search
- Light grey text on white that looks elegant but can't be read

**Practise:** Take your signature moment and design its touch version and its reduced-motion version. Both should still feel like the same idea. (`pnpm kit study for-everyone`)

**In my pins**

- `iva-n-red` Brightened Gabagool red: Contrast decided a colour: too dark for black text
- `lib-gn-spine` Gionatan Nese — About text on a centre spine, bending around a chrome figure: Everything drawn in WebGL, with an sr-only copy of the text behind it
- `iva-q-nav` Nav over the full-screen dots: The inverting nav got hard to read over the dots

<a id="decide-by-prototype"></a>
### Decide with real prototypes

**Compare working versions side by side, then choose.**

When you can't decide, build two or three real versions and switch between them. A working prototype in the browser shows timing, scroll and feel that a static mockup hides. It's how most of Iva's decisions got made.

**How to check:** Is there a decision you've been stuck on for more than a day? Build the options as switchable variants instead of thinking about it more.

**Usual mistakes**

- Deciding motion from a still image
- Polishing one option before comparing it with the others
- Throwing away the rejected versions instead of keeping them as pins

**Practise:** Build one section in two variants with a small switcher bar, and ask someone which one they'd keep and why. (`pnpm kit study decide-by-prototype`)

**In my pins**

- `lib-idea-variants` Build switchable variants to decide: Switchable variants beat static mockups every time
- `iva-q-work` Work section: Rows, Index or Strips?: Rows, Index or Strips: three work sections built to compare
- `iva-q-version` Grid version or full-screen version?: Two whole versions live behind a switcher
